newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hewlett-Packard sees Asian sales growing 30 percent/year.
newsitem.headline: Hewlett-Packard sees Asian sales growing 30 percent/year.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co. expects its Asia-Pacific revenues to keep growing at around 30 percent a year, the head of its worldwide geographic operations said Thursday.
Alan Bickell told reporters the Asia-Pacific region was growing rapidly because many of the company's best and most advanced new products are being developed there.
HP's turnover in the Asia-Pacific region, which has its headquarters in Hong Kong, was about $5 billion in 1995 out of a worldwide total of around $31.5 billion, he said.
The company's recent growth in the region had been "in excess of 30 percent" a year, he said. "I don't see that changing too much."

"Asia-Pacific will obviously have an increasing share of HP's manufacturing base," he said. "We don't seem to be able to expand our facilities rapidly enough to take care of the growth of our business."
Bickell, in Singapore to open the company's new $177 million Singapore factory, said HP would continue to transfer products to the Asia-Pacific region.

"Our growth rates in Asia-Pacific have consistently exceeded those of any other market that we have, so our view is that this will become an increasingly important and a larger and larger part of HP's overall sales," he said.

HP, which has around 60 percent of the world ink-jet printer market and up to 65 percent of the laser-jet market, has built a large research and development team in Singapore which is developing HP's "hand-held products," such as mini-computers, mobile printers and calculators.

"This is where the market is going. These are not products which are nearing the end of their life-cycle," he said. "These are products that basically are feeding into what we believe is going to be the exciting market of the 21st century -- the true information age."

Bickell said HP had been rationalising its Asia-Pacific operations, moving high value-added activities such as R&D, planning and high-technology products to countries such as Singapore which have highly-skilled, highly-waged populations.
More labour-intensive manufacturing was being moved to cheaper environments such as India, Indonesia and the Philippines, he said.
